transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-09
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Laura (Redwood SE), Mike (Aurora CTO), Priya (Aurora Lead ML), Jason (Aurora Infra), Lena (Aurora Product)

Summary (auto): POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscaling for an Aurora Systems POC. Goals: define success criteria (latency/throughput/cost), sizing for reserved GPUs, burst strategy, fallback policies, and a benchmark plan. Action items and timeline agreed.

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intros?
[00:06] Mike: sure — mike torres, cto at aurora systems. we've got priya, lead ml, and jason infra. lena product is here too.
[00:12] Samir: awesome. i'm samir, ae at redwood, and laura is our se, she'll drive the bench and tech details.
[00:18] Laura: hi all, excited to dig in. wanted to align first on scope — are we scoping a 6‑8 week pilot?
[00:24] Lena: yes we were thinking 6 weeks, must show latency at scale and cost feasibility for customers.
[00:30] Priya: our core workload is a chat assistant for support ticket triage — prompts avg 400 tokens, response avg 700 tokens, with a small tail to 2k for long contexts.
[00:38] Samir: good, that's helpful. can you share expected request patterns — steady vs spiky?
[00:42] Jason: it's pretty bursty — business hours spikes around 11am–2pm, peak concurrent requests around 120–200, baseline 30–40 qps. occasional promotional bursts to ~400 concurrent for a few hours.
[00:53] Laura: ok that helps. for a POC we usually propose a reserved baseline to guarantee throughput and a burst pool for short spikes.
[00:58] [01:00] Mike: what does reserved mean exactly — are those GPU reservations? and how fast can you scale?
[01:06] Samir: yes, reserved capacity = dedicated GPUs for your POC (no noisy neighbor). we size baseline to meet SLOs for typical traffic. autoscale can add burst capacity from a mix of reserved pool or elastic workers; warm up time depends on instance type but we can use warm standbys for <30s scale ups, or prewarmed containers for <10s in many regions.
[01:23] Priya: important — we need end‑to‑end p95 latency under 1.2s for single-turn small prompts and p95 under 2.5s for average ticket flows.
[01:31] Laura: noted. can you confirm token limits? you said avg 400+700 total ~1.1k tokens per call?
[01:36] Priya: yes, that's typical. some trajectories use conversation history up to 6k tokens but rare.
[01:42] Laura: ok. quick back‑of‑envelope: for your baseline 120 concurrent with avg 1.1k tokens, with model variant 'redwood-13b-q4' (we'll verify model later) and batching we expect X tokens/sec per GPU; to be conservative we'd propose reserving 4 GPUs for baseline and allow burst to 8 GPUs.
[01:58] Jason: 4 GPUs baseline feels high — can you show the math so we can justify cost?
[02:02] Samir: yeah i'll walk through it in the followup doc but rough calc: with batching + KV caching we get ~3–4x throughput vs single‑request cases. assume steady requests 40 qps * 1.1k tokens = 44k tokens/sec incoming; with 1 GPU handling ~12–15k tokens/sec (model dependent) you'd need ~3–4 GPUs. at peak 200 concurrent we'd need burst capacity of 7–8 GPUs.
[02:22] [02:30] Laura: another lever is model variant and quantization — moving from 13b to a 7b quantized variant drops latency and increases throughput significantly, but could affect quality. part of the POC is making an eval set to measure quality delta.
[02:40] Priya: yes that's critical. our success criteria is 1) maintain p95 latency targets, 2) maintain NLU quality within 3% F1 drop vs baseline model, 3) cost per 1k requests under $X (we'll provide target).
[02:52] Samir: those are good measurable criteria. for fallback we propose a tiered policy: primary = reserved 13b, fallback = quantized 13b or 7b variant, then degraded mode that returns hybrid cached responses or a cached summary.
[03:04] Mike: for regulatory reasons we need data not to leave region and KMS control for keys. can you run private or VPC?
[03:10] Laura: yes — Redwood Private supports VPC peering and customer KMS/HSM. for the POC we can run in our dedicated region with VPC peering to your cloud, or do a Private short trial on your infra.
[03:20] Jason: if we do VPC peering, what's network egress like and cold start implications?
[03:24] Samir: egress is normal cloud traffic; cold starts depend on instance type — for GPU workers cold-starts can be 30–120s if unprepared. to avoid that we recommend a warm pool (small number of prewarmed instances) or fast preemption with snapshot restore. We'll document exact timings after benchmarking.
[03:38] [03:50] Priya: for benchmarks we want to run at the real token distribution, including a small percentage of long‑history queries. can you support both openloop and closedloop tests?
[03:58] Laura: yes — our harness supports openloop TPS tests and closedloop conversational sims. we also capture per‑token cost, KV cache hit rate, batching stats and tail latencies.
[04:10] Lena: timeline — we need a customer-ready report at week 6 and decision at week 8. so bench week should be week 3–4.
[04:18] Samir: sounds good. proposed pilot timeline: week 0–1 setup + config, week 2 ingest prompts + tune batching/quantization, week 3 run baseline benchmarks, week 4 iterate, week 5 run full production sim, week 6 deliver report and run exec demo.
[04:33] Mike: what about reliability and fallback policy specifics — if reserved pool is exhausted do you throttle or route to a cheaper model?
[04:40] Laura: good q. recommended policy: 1) attempt scale within reserved pool; 2) if capacity exceeded, route to compatible quantized variant in burst pool; 3) if still constrained, enable degraded responses (short summaries or cached answers) or queue with a guaranteed SLA for high‑priority traffic. We can tag traffic by priority.
[04:56] Jason: how do you ensure correctness when switching models? prompt engineering might be needed to minimize drift.
[05:02] Priya: yes we need deterministic A/B comparisons. can redwood do canary rollouts and score metrics automatically?
[05:08] Laura: yes, console supports canaries, A/B, and quality regression alerts tied to your eval set. we can automatically route X% traffic to the fallback model and measure F1, hallucination, latency.
[05:20] [05:30] Mike: curious about cost controls — can we cap burst usage?
[05:34] Samir: absolutely — policies can cap max burst GPUs or spend per hour. also you can set per‑route budgets so customer facing routes can't blow budget.
[05:42] Priya: regarding caching — how do prefix/KV caches help with our conversational workload?
[05:46] Laura: KV cache primarily avoids recomputing earlier tokens for long contexts when the model reuses past computations. prefix caching can serve repeated system prompts or boilerplate, cutting token compute significantly. for triage flows we expect 20–30% token compute reduction if history is reused a lot.
[05:58] Jason: what about quantization impacts on memory and throughput? any recommended quant profiles?
[06:02] Laura: we typically test q4 and q8 routes; q4_0 or q4_k4 depending on model. q4 often gives best throughput while preserving quality for many tasks. we'll include quantization profiles in the bench matrix.
[06:12] [06:20] Samir: ok practical items — for the POC we'll need: 1) a sample of 2k prompts representative of requests, 2) target SLOs and cost ceiling, 3) shortlist of models to test.
[06:30] Priya: we'll share prompts and SLOs by friday 2025-09-12.
[06:34] Lena: we also want a clear rollback plan if quality drops in production.
[06:38] Laura: rollback is policy-driven — instant route change back to baseline model or increase caching. the console lets you automate fallback thresholds (e.g., if F1 drops >3% revert).
[06:48] [07:00] Mike: one more question on the burst strategy — do you prefer autoscaling up additional GPUs (cold workers) or bursting to a managed pool across regions?
[07:08] Samir: both are options. autoscaling to cold workers is cheaper but has slower ramp. managed burst pools with prewarmed instances in other regions can provide faster scale but may have slightly higher cost and egress. We usually recommend a hybrid: reserved baseline + local warm standbys + cross‑region burst for extreme events.
[07:26] Jason: what about regional failover — if a region is saturated do you have automatic reroute?
[07:30] Laura: yes we can route by policy. we also support model-compatible fallbacks to ensure same API surface. There is a short latency penalty for cross‑region traffic.
[07:40] [07:50] Priya: benchmarks — what's in the standard report?
[07:52] Laura: per-route p50/p90/p95 latencies, tokens/sec per GPU, cost per 1k requests, cache hit rates, batch size distribution, tail jitter, and quality metrics vs your eval set. we also include a recommended capacity plan.
[08:05] Samir: i'll attach a sample report in the followup.
[08:08] Mike: for KPIs, we'll look at latency SLO, cost per 1k, and quality delta. If you hit targets we move to a 6‑12 month reserved commit.
[08:18] Lena: can you also include an appendix with SOC2 and encryption info?
[08:22] Samir: yes we'll send security whitepapers and SOC2 certs.
[08:26] [08:30] Priya: ok, operationally, do we need any special IAM or roles?
[08:34] Laura: we'll request a service account for the bench runner and a read‑only role for metrics; RBAC is flexible.
[08:40] Jason: about the warm pool size — how many warm workers do you recommend?
[08:44] Laura: depends on burstiness — for your pattern I'd suggest 2–4 warm GPUs locally to reduce cold start risk, plus a cross‑region burst of 4–6 if needed. we'll tune after first run.
[08:56] [09:00] Mike: i'm concerned about model switching causing subtle behavior differences. how long will you run quality tests before switching traffic?
[09:06] Laura: canary windows are configurable; for POC we usually do 10–20k requests over 24–48 hours and then evaluate metrics. Rapid canary (1–2 hours) is possible for non-critical routes.
[09:18] Priya: do you store logs and audit trails for requests? that's a compliance ask.
[09:22] Samir: yes audit logs and per‑token billing traces are available; we can filter PII and route logs to your log sink.
[09:30] [09:40] Jason: network constraints — if we do Private on prem how long to set up?
[09:44] Laura: Private deployments typically take 2–4 weeks for initial setup depending on infra and entitlements; for the POC we can do a hosted dedicated setup faster (~3–5 business days) to start benching.
[09:54] Samir: given timelines you proposed earlier, hosted dedicated pilot with VPC peering seems fastest.
[09:58] Lena: agreed.
[10:00] [10:10] Priya: for the benchmark run we want both high‑priority and low‑priority traffic mixes, to test routing policies.
[10:14] Laura: we'll create traffic profiles and include priority tagging and budget caps in the bench.
[10:20] Samir: one more point — we recommend instrumenting synthetic golden queries so you have deterministic health checks and can detect regressions quickly.
[10:28] Priya: ok we'll add golden queries to the prompt set.
[10:32] Mike: any blockers from your side to start?
[10:34] Laura: from our side we need the prompt set, SLOs/cost ceiling, and VPC details if you're peering. once we have that we can schedule bench week.
[10:44] [10:50] Samir: recap of next steps — we will send: 1) proposed capacity diagram (baseline+burst sizes) + pricing, 2) benchmark harness and runbook, 3) security docs (SOC2/KMS/RBAC), 4) sample reporting template. You (Aurora) will send prompts, SLOs, and VPC info.
[11:06] Lena: timeline sounds good. let's aim to have sample prompts and SLOs by 2025-09-12.
[11:12] Priya: agreed.
[11:14] Mike: thanks all. excited to see the bench.
[11:18] Samir: thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench window and a doc with numbers.
[11:22] Laura: we'll also include quantization test matrix and recommended warm pool sizes.
[11:26] Mike: perfect.
[11:30] [11:35] (call ends)
